Stand and look

Line of sight (today's ground, no trees): from the yard only the top ~2 m of Festival Hall's dome clears the ridge at Oakland Ave; from upstairs about 45 m of it. The 2-story Forest Park Hotel hid the Ferris wheel and Horticulture. These views switch off the 1903 park layer, since it is not known whether the park still stood in 1904.

Rides

The wheel turns once in about 4 minutes here; a real ride took about 20 minutes. Bicycles are a convenience for exploring, not a 1904 feature: visitors walked, rode the Intramural Railway, or hired rolling chairs. While walking: B = get on or off a nearby bicycle, R = board or leave the wheel when you are near it.

Key (map colors)

Frame building (1904) Brick building (1904) Fireproof building (1904) 1904 Grand Basin, Water Ways and lakes (ground plan) Today's lakes (2017 lidar; shown as you slide to today) Philippine Reservation buildings (ground plan) Philippine village areas (dwellings not drawn on the plan) West End Heights (1903) Still standing (Brookings Hall, Art Museum…) Today's streets
Heights are estimates from building size, not from the maps. The terrain is today's (2017 lidar), not the 1904 ground. Facades, roofs and trees are illustrative: the palaces were white “staff” plaster, but window and arch patterns here are generic, and no map records 1904 tree positions (trees are placed by density rules: dense groves in unused parkland, sparse on the formal grounds, scattered on farmland). The grounds beyond the insurance maps in the fair's southwest quarter (Live Stock, Camping Grounds, Forestry plots, Nursery, Plant Industry and Irrigation exhibits, the Anthropology grounds, and the Physical Culture stadium that survives as Washington University's Francis Field) are traced from the same ground plan, which drew most of them only as outlined areas, so they appear as tinted ground. The Anthropology grounds held living exhibits of Native American and other Indigenous peoples. Visitors are illustrative too: about 13,000 figures in typical 1904 dress (dark suits with boaters or bowlers; long skirts, white shirtwaists and wide hats, some with parasols) placed by density rules, densest along palace fronts; real attendance averaged roughly 100,000 a day. The fair's water comes from the ground plan: the Grand Basin and the ring of “Water Way” lagoons around the palaces (about 9 hectares, crossed by bridges), the cascades, the U.S. Life Saving exhibit lake, Arrowhead Lake at the Philippine Reservation and smaller ponds; the insurance maps drew only the banks. Sliding to today brings in today's lakes from the 2017 lidar: today's Emerson Grand Basin lies on the 1904 basin's site and several of today's waterways follow the old lagoon banks, while the Post-Dispatch Lake (dug in 1894) took its present shape later — two 1904 palaces stood on part of it. The Life Saving lake's site is dry ground today. Buildings that still stand (Brookings Hall, which served as the fair's Administration Building, a neighbouring Washington University building, and the Palace of Fine Arts, now the Art Museum) stay visible when you slide to today; Brookings' tower height is an estimate. The Pike, the fair's mile of amusements, ran along the north side of today's Lindell Boulevard, west of the main entrance at DeBaliviere (today's Missouri History Museum), and turned at Skinker; houses now stand on its site. The Philippine Reservation comes from the 1903–04 official ground plan (Library of Congress), which drew its buildings, lake and paths but only labelled the village areas; nearly 1,200 Filipinos lived there during the fair, and more than a dozen died. Sources: Library of Congress Sanborn maps (1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition; St. Louis vol. 10, 1903) and Ground Plan, Louisiana Purchase Exposition (Carson & Brown, Oct. 1903); USGS 3DEP lidar; USGS/Census streets.
